scoreNote: Strong (5): a recommendation-appropriate response that shows why mass benefit cannot be predicted and why a head-count standard neglects the few, then concedes a legitimate role for weighing benefit; well argued.

sentences.text: With limited money and talent, it seems only sensible to point science at the problems that would help the most people.
The recommendation makes this a rule, urging scientists to focus their research on areas likely to benefit the greatest number.

The recommendation is appealing and partly right, but as a governing principle it would do real harm, because the most beneficial discoveries are often unpredictable and the neediest people are not always the most numerous.
First, the recommendation assumes we can know in advance which research will benefit the most people, and usually we cannot.
The most world-changing discoveries — electricity, the structure of DNA, the mathematics behind computers — began as curiosity-driven work with no foreseeable application.
Had scientists been required to justify their benefit to the masses beforehand, much of this research would never have been funded, and the benefits would never have arrived.
Directing all research toward foreseeable mass benefit would therefore starve precisely the basic science from which the largest benefits unpredictably flow.
The laser was once a solution in search of a problem; today it is everywhere, in surgery, in communication, and in industry.
A policy that funded only the obviously useful would, ironically, sacrifice the discoveries that prove most useful of all.
Moreover, a focus on the greatest number would abandon people whose needs are real but rare.
A strict head-count standard would steer research toward common conditions and away from rare diseases that afflict only thousands, leaving those sufferers with no hope at all.
Yet a person with a rare illness is no less deserving of a cure than one with a common cold, and a just society does not measure the worth of research solely by how many it helps.
The same logic would neglect the distant future, since people not yet born cannot be counted among today's greatest number, even though research now may save them later.
Climate and pandemic research benefit chiefly the people of the future, who do not appear in any present tally of beneficiaries.
Counting heads is a poor way to decide whose suffering matters.
However, the recommendation does point at something legitimate.
Where two equally promising projects compete for the same scarce funds, the likely scale of benefit is a perfectly reasonable thing to weigh.
But weighing benefit among options is very different from making mass benefit the sole focus of all research, which is what the recommendation proposes.
A wise science policy funds a broad portfolio — applied work aimed at present needs and basic work whose payoffs cannot yet be seen — rather than betting everything on the foreseeable.
To serve the most people in the long run, science must be free to pursue more than what serves the most people now.
In conclusion, scientists should consider the benefit of their work without being confined to whatever helps the largest number.
Because the greatest discoveries are unforeseeable and the neediest are not always the most numerous, a rule of mass benefit would impoverish science and neglect the vulnerable.
The surest way to benefit the greatest number is to let science explore widely, including the questions whose usefulness no one can yet predict.
